Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma, the trigger pattern is difficult to reconcile clinically: explosion/bang sounds and hospital/antiseptic smells imply very different trauma contexts or aftermaths, with no accompanying memory or appraisal content linking them into a coherent assault narrative. This is more than merely unusual because the trigger set suggests mixed trauma cues rather than one assault profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' does not fit well with the rest of the profile. Threat items focus on immediate environmental danger and startle, while memory items center on grief, auditory recall, and emotional numbing; none support a prominent bodily injury theme. In the absence of corroborating assault-related injury cues, this appraisal appears mismatched.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: Given the very strong Triggers → Threat edge, trigger items should plausibly feed the specific threat pattern. 'Being naked' can fit vulnerability and danger, but explosion sounds and hospital smells do not connect well to the selected threat items for a single assault formulation, making the trigger-to-threat linkage clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma, hospital/antiseptic smell is only coherent if the assault involved serious injury or hospital treatment, but nothing in threat, memory, or appraisals anchors the trauma to a medical context. In this profile it stands out as insufficiently connected to the rest of the formulation.

'Being naked' as a trigger implies a sexual assault, humiliation, medical exposure, or a very specific vulnerability context. The other items do not support that context: threat items reflect generalized hypervigilance/startle, memory items do not indicate bodily violation or exposure, and appraisals focus on self-blame/protection of others rather than sexualized shame. This makes the trigger hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

For an assault trauma, 'being naked' as a trigger is not impossible, but without any corroborating memory, threat, or appraisal content suggesting sexual assault, humiliation, or clothing-related vulnerability, it stands out as poorly integrated with the rest of the profile. The other trigger items point to alcohol cues and loss of control, while threat items center on hypervigilance/startle; this specific trigger appears disconnected from the described trauma representation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed
issues.explanation: 'I should have protected others and I failed' implies the patient experienced the assault in a protector/caretaker role or alongside endangered others. No memory, trigger, or threat item references other people being harmed or the patient's responsibility toward them. The rest of the appraisals are self-focused incompetence/blame, so this item is the main cross-node inconsistency.

vignette:
Samuel came to treatment at 77 after months of urging from his wife, who had watched him grow more brittle and watchful in ways that did not fit the calm authority he had carried through decades as a school principal. The assault had happened a little over a year earlier, late one evening after a district function. He had stayed behind at the school to finish paperwork in his office, then walked out to the parking lot alone. A man approached him asking for money, and before Samuel could step away or make sense of what was happening, he was cornered beside his car. What remained most vivid was not only the physical threat but the feeling of being overpowered and directed by someone else’s commands. He could still remember being told what to do, where to move, when to hand things over, and the unbearable knowledge that he was no longer in charge of his own body or choices. The man had been drinking; Samuel remembered the sour smell of alcohol on his breath as clearly as anything else. Even now, that smell could pull him back instantly.

In the first weeks afterward, Samuel told himself he should be able to handle it. He had spent a lifetime being composed in crises, the person teachers and families relied on when something went wrong. But when memories came, they arrived in strange and uneven ways. At times he would remember the assault and be flooded with grief so strong it startled him, grief not only for the attack itself but for what felt lost in him afterward. At other times he could describe the event in a flat, detached way, as if he were recounting something that had happened to another man. He found this especially disturbing. He would hear, in his head, fragments of the assailant’s voice and the sounds from the parking lot that night, so sharply that for a moment the present seemed thin and unreliable.

At school, his symptoms became woven into the structure of his day. Samuel still insisted on arriving early and walking the halls before students came in, but now whenever he entered a classroom, the auditorium, a parent meeting, even the cafeteria, his eyes went first to the exits. He noted doors, side doors, who was standing near them, whether anything blocked his path. If a student moved suddenly beside him in a corridor, or a staff member stepped unexpectedly into his office doorway, his body reacted before he could think, with a violent jolt of alarm that embarrassed him. He hated that the children could sometimes see it. During evening events he became especially tense. If a parent leaned in too quickly, or if he caught the smell of alcohol on someone’s breath at a fundraiser or after a sports banquet, he felt himself tighten all over. He began avoiding some district social functions entirely, offering excuses about fatigue.

What Samuel said most often in session was that he could no longer rely on himself. He had come to believe that on the one night he most needed sound judgment, he had failed himself. He replayed small decisions from that evening—staying late, walking out alone, responding before he had fully assessed the man—and these details had taken on the force of evidence that the event happened because of the way he acted. At the same time, he was certain he could not rely on other people either. He noticed how quickly help had failed to appear in the parking lot, and now in daily life he felt uneasy depending on staff, security measures, or even familiar community members. If someone suggested, “Let me handle this,” something in him recoiled. Being directed, hurried, or pressured, even in ordinary situations, could bring up the same sick sense of losing control.

At home, this had narrowed his life. His wife found that simple requests could unexpectedly unsettle him if he experienced them as being pushed. He would not say that directly; instead he became quiet, stubborn, or abruptly withdrawn. She missed the ease with which they used to go out together. He sat in restaurants only if he could choose the table, usually one with a clear view of the door. In crowded places he remained tense, reacting sharply to motion at his side. The man who had once been warmly available to students and staff now seemed perpetually braced.

He finally agreed to seek help after a school assembly, when a student rushing backstage brushed past him from the side and Samuel spun around so abruptly that several teachers stopped and stared. Later that same week, he caught the smell of alcohol on a visitor in the front office and had to retreat to his room and close the door, shaken and ashamed. What frightened him most was not only feeling afraid but feeling altered—older, less dependable, less able to trust his own judgment or the people around him. What he hoped for, though he said it cautiously, was to be able to walk through his own school and his own life without constantly preparing for danger, and without feeling that the man in the parking lot had taken something permanent from him.
